source.title: On data and parameters of pre-trained neural networks for solar power forecasting
source.authors: Robbe Vander Eeckt; Joris Depoortere; H. Kazmi

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some equation and page-break formatting is garbled, but this does not prevent extraction of the reported results.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests scaling behavior in zero-shot solar forecasting transfer and reports that performance plateaus or decreases beyond eight years of source data, rather than continuing to improve. It also reports no strong relationship between source-data quantity and selected model complexity.
record.gate_note: The study reports a qualitative nRMSE trend in text and shows the plotted values only in Fig. 3; exact values are not available in the supplied text. Table III reports median selected hyperparameters by source-data duration, not parameter counts. The 36% comparison with persistence and the integrated-gradient findings do not themselves test a scaling-law version.
record.test_reason: The study pre-trains LSTMs on 1, 2, 4, 8 and 15 years of simulated PV source data and reports zero-shot target nRMSE against data volume. This is a new setting (time-series transfer) bearing on V5. The authors explicitly contrast the result with neural scaling laws. However, they fit no power law, cover only about one order of magnitude of data, and give the trend only in prose and Fig. 3, so the test is weak.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find that zero-shot performance improves with source data only up to about eight years, where the best model beats persistence by about 36%. They find that selected model size was not strongly correlated with data quantity, which deviates from scaling-law expectations. They tentatively attribute the plateau to a transfer gap and possible multicollinear features, and call for testing larger architectures such as transformers.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates zero-shot transfer for solar-power forecasting with LSTMs, varying source-data duration and measuring nRMSE; it does not reproduce language-model loss or compute scaling measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported performance trend depends on source-data quantity: improvement is reported through eight years, then plateaus or decreases.

fits_no_version.finding: Median hyperparameters selected by Optuna stay in a similar range from 1 to 15 years of source data. The authors say model size was not strongly correlated with data quantity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal model size selected by hyperparameter search grows with training-data volume.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE PES Innovative Smart Grid Technologies Conference Europe
record.problems: The study evaluates 10 geographically close target sites and reports forecast nRMSE rather than pretraining cross-entropy loss. Exact performance values are not stated in the supplied text, and the reported hyperparameters do not give parameter counts.

untested.parts: No power-law form is fitted. Data volume spans only about 1 order of magnitude, and parameters and compute are not varied systematically. In-domain (source) loss is not reported, and other modalities, repeated data and fine-tuning are not tested.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No fitted exponents and no comparison of fitting or setup choices.

missing.what: Median and quartile nRMSE per source-data duration (1, 2, 4, 8, 15 years), plotted only in Fig. 3. These are needed to judge whether the 1–8 year trend is power-law-like and how large the post-8-year change is.

record.verdict_notes: The plateau of zero-shot target error under distribution shift is compatible with scaling laws for transfer (Hernandez et al.) plus an irreducible term, as the authors themselves hint. It is therefore treated as limits_scope rather than challenges. The evidence is a textual trend description only.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
It does not fit laws on smaller runs and evaluate predictions against much larger runs.
There is no fixed-compute-budget comparison or estimate of parameter- and token-optimal allocations.
It does not compare depth, width, or other architecture choices at a fixed parameter count.
The study examines solar forecasting transfer using nRMSE, not cross-entropy loss, and does not test other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer beyond this setting.
It does not test downstream task performance as a function of model scale or pretraining loss.
It does not compare fitting methods or parameter-counting conventions, estimate fitted exponents, or test whether compute-optimal allocations depend on setup.

rows.operation_detail: Compared forecast nRMSE across models pre-trained with varying amounts of source data.
rows.value: Performance improves as source data increases up to 8 years, after which it plateaus or decreases; exact plotted values are not stated.
rows.uncertainty: 25%-quantile and 75%-quantile over sites are shown; exact values are not stated.
rows.note: This is the authors' textual description of the aggregate trend across source-data amounts; it is not a reported power-law fit.
rows.check: V7 link removed. The study fits no exponents and compares no fitting or setup choices, so a qualitative plateau in zero-shot transfer error says nothing about fit-dependence. Partial is kept for V5: error improves from 1 to 8 years, then plateaus or worsens. No baseline is given for the data trend; persistence nRMSE (11.78%) is a forecasting baseline, not a scaling baseline.

relationships.condition: Small LSTM, zero-shot transfer from simulated to real PV generation at 10 nearby Dutch sites, 1–15 years of source data
relationships.reason: Target nRMSE improves only up to 8 years, then plateaus or decreases. No power-law fit is given, and the authors attribute the plateau to a transfer gap (r1).
relationships.display_finding: Target nRMSE improved only through eight years of source data, after which transfer gains plateaued or diminished, which the authors attributed to a transfer gap.
